facts.claim: Bright Eyes released a cover of John Prine's 'Christmas in Prison' on December 6, 2023, with vocals from Prine.
The single is credited as ℗ 2023 Oh Boy Records, marketed and distributed by Thirty Tigers.
Conor Oberst, Mike Mogis and Nate Walcott are named as the Bright Eyes members behind this version.
Prine's voice on the track is a sample from his 1993 release A John Prine Christmas, not a new recording. The sample is a spoken-word monologue in which Prine reflects on past Christmases.
NME describes the track as atmospheric and country-tinged, with Oberst's echoey vocal accentuated by plaintive pedal steel guitar.
Prine originally recorded the song for his 1973 album Sweet Revenge.
Oberst said it was strange to share a track with a hero who has died, that this is normally not something he would do, and that he doesn't like holograms.
Oberst said Prine 'really changed my life on a lot of levels.' He said that hearing the sample of Prine talking about Christmas made him smile and he wanted to share it.

Proceeds from the single go to Prine's charity, The Hello In There Foundation, and to four of its 2023 grantees: Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition, Porters Call, National Coalition for Homeless Veterans, and Renewal House.
A Prine x Oberst holiday ornament was sold alongside the single, with proceeds also going to The Hello In There Foundation.

research.lineage: A Bright Eyes indie-folk cover of a John Prine country-folk Christmas song, built around a sample of Prine's own voice and released through Prine's Oh Boy Records to benefit his charity.

draft:
The turkey is real good, and the pistols are "carved out of wood." That's how John Prine opened **Christmas in Prison** on his 1973 album *Sweet Revenge*: a joke delivered so flatly you almost miss the escape plan inside it. Bright Eyes keep that deadpan intact. Their version, made by Conor Oberst, Mike Mogis and Nate Walcott, adds one thing nobody else could: Prine himself, talking.

The song's narrator is locked up and in love, and the two facts keep tripping over each other. "I dream of her always, even when I don't dream" is a lovely, dizzy line. The longing is so constant it doesn't need sleep. The chorus swings the other way into bravado, with old mother nature having "nothing on me" and the couple "rolling" and "flowing, by God." It's the swagger of someone who can't afford to sound as lonely as he is. Then come the comparisons, which get stranger and sweeter as they go: a chess game with someone he admires, a picnic in the rain after a prairie fire, saccharin at a drugstore sale. They're funny, but they're also the sound of a man reaching for anything to keep her vivid.

Oberst sings it clear and relaxed over a steady acoustic guitar pattern, the groove slow and swaying. Voices stack around him, one an octave below and one above, in three parts. The room sounds warm and close, more like a kitchen than a stage.

In the middle, the song stops for Prine. The voice comes from his 1993 record *A John Prine Christmas*, a spoken monologue about the Montgomery Ward catalogue arriving in late August, eating a red ornament at three because he thought it was an apple, and finding a dark aqua Silvertone guitar under the tree. He posed in the mirror like Elvis until his brother Dave taught him a couple of chords. "Now I'm here in your living room," he says, and laughs. Oberst has said it's strange to share a track with a hero who has died, that he doesn't like holograms. He used the sample anyway because hearing Prine talk about Christmas made him smile. That smile is all over the recording. Prine ends the talk by telling you to slip a stranger a buck, and the single's proceeds go to his Hello In There Foundation and four of its grantees.

The last verse brings back the prison yard, with a searchlight swinging like a gun across the snow. Then the narrator signs off with "And I'll probably get homesick, I love you, goodnight." He tucks the sadness into the middle of the line, between a shrug and a kiss.

The song lets a man in a cell and a man who's gone both say goodnight like they'll be back tomorrow, and you're left holding the homesickness neither of them will say out loud.

factCheck.claim: The turkey is real good, and the pistols are "carved out of wood."
factCheck.note: The lyric is 'the food was real good / We had turkey and pistols carved out of wood.' Changed to 'food' so it matches. The 'carved out of wood' quote is exact.

factCheck.claim: Prine opened Christmas in Prison on his 1973 album Sweet Revenge with those lines
factCheck.note: Prine originally recorded the song for Sweet Revenge in 1973. The lyrics open with these lines.

factCheck.claim: A joke delivered so flatly you almost miss the escape plan; Bright Eyes keep that deadpan intact
factCheck.note: Nothing describes how Prine's original was delivered, and 'deadpan' goes beyond the listening notes. Reframed around the joke and the relaxed vocal, which the passes support.

factCheck.claim: Version made by Conor Oberst, Mike Mogis and Nate Walcott, with Prine himself talking
factCheck.note: Rolling Stone names the three. NME says Prine's voice is a sample of a spoken monologue.

factCheck.claim: "I dream of her always, even when I don't dream"
Chorus quotes: "nothing on me", "rolling", "flowing, by God"
factCheck.note: The words are in the lyrics, but the review had too many quoted lyric lines. Paraphrased the chorus and kept three quotes in total.

factCheck.claim: Comparisons: chess game with someone he admires, picnic in the rain after a prairie fire, saccharin at a drugstore sale
factCheck.note: All three images are in the lyrics.

factCheck.claim: Oberst sings it clear and relaxed over a steady acoustic guitar pattern, slow and swaying groove
factCheck.note: All three passes agree on a clear, relaxed male lead, a steady acoustic guitar and a gentle swaying groove. NME names Oberst's vocal.

factCheck.claim: Three-part vocals, one an octave below and one above
factCheck.note: All passes agree on a higher harmony. Passes 1 and 3 give the octave-lower voice.

factCheck.claim: Room sounds warm and close, more like a kitchen than a stage
factCheck.note: Passes 1 and 2 say warm, passes 1 and 3 say intimate and close. 'Kitchen' is the critic's comparison.

factCheck.claim: In the middle the song stops for Prine; the sample comes from his 1993 record A John Prine Christmas, a spoken monologue
factCheck.note: NME supports the 1993 source and the monologue. The lyric structure puts the monologue between the choruses and the final verse.

factCheck.claim: Monologue details: Montgomery Ward catalogue in late August, red ornament at three mistaken for an apple, aqua Silvertone under the tree, mirror and Elvis, brother Dave taught chords
"Now I'm here in your living room," he says, and laughs
factCheck.note: The line is accurate and the lyrics show a laugh. Paraphrased to stay within the three-quote limit.

factCheck.claim: Oberst said it's strange to share a track with a hero who has died and that he doesn't like holograms; he used the sample because Prine talking about Christmas made him smile
Prine ends the talk by telling you to slip a stranger a buck
factCheck.note: The slip-a-buck advice isn't the end of the monologue. Reworded to 'before the talk is done.'

factCheck.claim: Proceeds go to his Hello In There Foundation and four of its grantees
The last verse brings back the prison yard, searchlight swinging like a gun across the snow
factCheck.note: The lyric is 'searchlight in the big yard swings round like a gun' and the spotlight on the snowflakes. 'Brings back the yard' is wrong because the yard isn't mentioned earlier. Reworded.

factCheck.claim: "And I'll probably get homesick, I love you, goodnight."
A man in a cell and a man who's gone both say goodnight like they'll be back tomorrow
factCheck.note: Only the narrator says goodnight, and the sample doesn't. Rewrote the closing line to rest on supported material.
